newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka 1997 rubber output seen up, prices firm.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka 1997 rubber output seen up, prices firm.

text.p: Sri Lankan rubber production is expected to rise to 118 million kg this year after a 6.5 percent increase in prices in 1996, government officials said on Tuesday.

Despite a severe drought, the island's rubber crop rose to 112.5 million kg in 1996 from 105.7 million kg in 1995, P. Liyanarachchi, director-general of the Rubber Development Department, told Reuters.

"Production rose last year because high prices helped the industry," he said. "Now producers have more confidence in rubber. They're paying more attention to maintaining their lands now that they are getting better prices."
Dr. Keerthi Tillekeratne, director of the government Rubber Research Institute (RRI) said management firms running rubber estates had improved productivity after getting a longer lease on the land.

"The management firms are doing a better job," he told Reuters. "The use of rain guards has shown a clear improvement. High-yielding clones are also coming into bearing, while subsidy payments to small cultivators are being done very effectively."
Liyanarachchi said prices were expected to remain firm this year after soaring to record highs in the past two years.
"Prices are unlikely to drop. Natural rubber has a better demand now, with Western markets being more concerned about the environmental effects of using synthetic rubber," he said.
Prices have remained firm at recent Colombo auctions on fears of a production shortfall caused by "wintering", drought and the disruption of tapping when the rains come.
Wintering occurs when the tree goes into a period of hibernation during the dry months of the first quarter.
Small cultivators, who tap almost daily and produce the bulk of the crop, stop tapping to rest the trees during the January-March dry period, Liyanarachchi said.
Brokers and exporters say some factories work only half the day as their wells run dry because of drought.
"I do not think that production will come down because of drought," Liyanarachchi said. "Production rose in 1996 despite a severe drought."
Tillekeratne said that while quality might decline because of the water shortage, quantities were not likely to be affected.
"Rubber is the only crop which does better in drought," he said.
Sri Lanka produces just two percent of the world natural rubber output and has slipped from being the world's fourth biggest rubber producer to eighth in 25 years.
Rubber production is forecast to rise to 126 million kg by 2000, Tillekeratne said.
Liyanarachchi said raw rubber exports rose to 72 million kg last year from 68 million kg in 1995.
Production of sheet rubber rose to 53 million kg in 1996 from 42 million kg in 1995, he said.

Latex crepe output rose to 33.7 million kg in 1996 from 29.3 million kg in 1995 while exports fell to 20.9 million kg from 21.3 million kg in 1995, reflecting an increase in consumption by local rubber-products manufacturers.
Sri Lanka is the sole producer of latex crepe, used for making surgical and pharmaceutical rubber products, infant toys and rubber goods used in contact with food.
